```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Leahy et al. (2020), Results, "Hypothesis 1": a 2 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA (design
# problem x fixation source) on the fixation ratio, i.e. concepts rated "similar" to the
# initial concept divided by all concepts, first (individual brainstorming) phase only.
#   Fixation source: self-generated (control) M = 0.32, SD = 0.24; provided example
#                    M = 0.24, SD = 0.28; F(1, 165) = 4.4, p < .04.
#   Problem:         no-spill cup M = 0.23, SD = 0.23; bike rack M = 0.33, SD = 0.29;
#                    F(1, 165) = 5.6, p < .02.
#   Interaction:     F(1, 165) < 1, ns.
# N = 166 concept sets were analysed ("Measuring Fixation"), although an error df of 165 in a
# 2 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA implies N = 169. The paper does not report the n per fixation-
# source group, so an even split (83 / 83) is assumed below: the original's 95% CI and
# Cohen's d are therefore approximations, while its F and p are as reported.
original <- list(
  groups = tibble(
    condition = c("control", "example"),
    n         = c(83, 83),
    mean      = c(0.32, 0.24),
    sd        = c(0.24, 0.28)
  ),
  F        = 4.4,
  df_error = 165,
  p_text   = "< .04"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Data layout this code expects:
#   data/raw/<experiment id>/participants.csv, trials.csv, errors.csv   from `npm run export`
#   data/coded/<experiment id>/ratings.csv                               from the coders:
#     one row per rated brainstorm concept, columns
#       participant_id   as in trials.csv
#       sheet_number     the concept's sheet number in the brainstorm phase
#       similar          1 if rated similar to that participant's initial concept, else 0
#                        (the final, reconciled rating)
# Until ratings.csv exists, everything up to the exclusions runs and the fixation analyses
# say they are waiting for the coding.

condition_labels <- c(control = "Self-generated (control)", example = "Provided example")

# Concept sheets as the participant left them. A sheet revisited from the "Go to" list has
# one row per visit (`revision` 1, 2, ...); the highest revision is its final version.
final_sheets <- function(trials) {
  needed <- c("task", "phase", "sheet_number", "revision", "empty")
  if (!all(needed %in% names(trials)) || !any(trials$task == "concept_sheet", na.rm = TRUE)) {
    return(tibble(participant_id = character(), phase = character(), sheet_number = integer(),
                  revision = integer(), empty = logical()))
  }
  trials |>
    filter(task == "concept_sheet") |>
    mutate(sheet_number = as.integer(sheet_number), revision = as.integer(revision),
           empty = as.logical(empty)) |>
    group_by(participant_id, phase, sheet_number) |>
    slice_max(revision, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    ungroup()
}

# Load one phase's exported data, apply the exclusion rule, and compute fixation scores if the
# ratings exist. Returns NULL if that phase has not been exported yet, which is how every
# section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 1e5)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE)
  sheets   <- final_sheets(trials)

  # Exclusion rule: replace with the rule you preregistered. Here, the minimum the fixation
  # ratio needs to be defined: at least one non-empty brainstorm concept, and (control group)
  # a non-empty initial concept to compare the brainstorm concepts with. The original also
  # removed concept sets in which students "failed to follow instructions or the completed
  # concepts were illegible or uninterpretable"; add that as a coder judgment if you use it.
  per_participant <- sheets |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_concepts  = sum(phase == "brainstorm" & empty %in% FALSE),
              has_initial = any(phase == "initial" & empty %in% FALSE),
              .groups = "drop")
  checked <- complete |>
    select(participant_id, condition, problem) |>
    left_join(per_participant, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(n_concepts  = replace_na(n_concepts, 0L),
           has_initial = replace_na(has_initial, FALSE),
           no_concepts = n_concepts == 0,
           no_initial  = condition == "control" & !has_initial)
  keep <- checked |> filter(!no_concepts, !no_initial)

  ratings_path <- file.path("..", "data", "coded", id, "ratings.csv")
  ratings <- if (file.exists(ratings_path)) read_csv(ratings_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors, sheets = sheets,
       complete = complete, keep = keep, ratings = ratings,
       scores = fixation_scores(keep, sheets, ratings),
       n_no_concepts = sum(checked$no_concepts), n_no_initial = sum(checked$no_initial & !checked$no_concepts))
}

# One row per analysed participant: fixation ratio = brainstorm concepts rated similar to the
# initial concept / all brainstorm concepts (Leahy et al., 2020, "Measuring Fixation").
# NULL until the ratings exist.
fixation_scores <- function(keep, sheets, ratings) {
  if (is.null(ratings)) return(NULL)
  concepts <- sheets |>
    filter(phase == "brainstorm", empty %in% FALSE, participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
    select(participant_id, sheet_number) |>
    left_join(ratings |> select(participant_id, sheet_number, similar),
              by = c("participant_id", "sheet_number"))
  n_unrated <- sum(is.na(concepts$similar))
  if (n_unrated > 0) message(n_unrated, " brainstorm concept(s) have no rating yet and are left out of the ratios.")
  concepts |>
    filter(!is.na(similar)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_rated = n(), n_similar = sum(similar == 1), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(ratio = n_similar / n_rated) |>
    inner_join(keep |> select(participant_id, condition, problem, n_concepts), by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = names(condition_labels)),
           problem   = factor(problem, levels = c("cup", "bike")))
}

# Mean, SD and n of the fixation ratio per fixation-source group.
group_summary <- function(scores) {
  scores |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(ratio), sd = sd(ratio), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(condition = as.character(condition))
}

# 2 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA with Type II sums of squares: each main effect is tested
# controlling for the other, which suits unequal cell sizes and (as in the original) an
# interaction that is expected to be small. The paper does not say which type it used.
fixation_anova <- function(scores) {
  rss <- function(m) sum(residuals(m)^2)
  two_problems <- n_distinct(scores$problem) == 2
  full <- if (two_problems) lm(ratio ~ condition * problem, scores) else lm(ratio ~ condition, scores)
  df_e <- df.residual(full)
  test <- function(effect, without, with) {
    ss <- rss(without) - rss(with)
    f  <- ss / (rss(full) / df_e)
    tibble(effect = effect, F = f, df = 1, df_error = df_e,
           p = pf(f, 1, df_e, lower.tail = FALSE), partial_eta2 = ss / (ss + rss(full)))
  }
  if (!two_problems) return(test("Fixation source", lm(ratio ~ 1, scores), full))
  additive <- lm(ratio ~ condition + problem, scores)
  bind_rows(test("Fixation source", lm(ratio ~ problem, scores), additive),
            test("Design problem", lm(ratio ~ condition, scores), additive),
            test("Source × problem", additive, full))
}

# The key statistic: difference in mean fixation ratio, self-generated minus provided
# (positive = the original's direction), with a 95% CI, Cohen's d (pooled SD), and the
# ANOVA main effect of fixation source. From group summaries alone (the original), the CI
# uses the pooled-df t interval and F, p are taken as given.
key_from_groups <- function(g, F, df_error, p, p_text = NULL, eta2 = NULL) {
  c_ <- g[g$condition == "control", ]
  e_ <- g[g$condition == "example", ]
  est <- c_$mean - e_$mean
  se  <- sqrt(c_$sd^2 / c_$n + e_$sd^2 / e_$n)
  pooled_sd <- sqrt(((c_$n - 1) * c_$sd^2 + (e_$n - 1) * e_$sd^2) / (c_$n + e_$n - 2))
  half <- qt(0.975, c_$n + e_$n - 2) * se
  tibble(N = c_$n + e_$n, m_control = c_$mean, sd_control = c_$sd, m_example = e_$mean, sd_example = e_$sd,
         estimate = est, ci_low = est - half, ci_high = est + half,
         F = F, df_error = df_error, p = p,
         p_text = p_text %||% format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         d = est / pooled_sd, partial_eta2 = eta2 %||% (F / (F + df_error)))
}
key_original <- function() key_from_groups(original$groups, original$F, original$df_error, NA, original$p_text)

# The same statistics from a phase's data. NULL until both groups have at least two
# analysed participants.
key_stats <- function(d) {
  s <- d$scores
  if (is.null(s) || any(table(s$condition) < 2)) return(NULL)
  g <- group_summary(s)
  a <- fixation_anova(s) |> filter(effect == "Fixation source")
  out <- key_from_groups(g, a$F, a$df_error, a$p, eta2 = a$partial_eta2)
  # Welch interval for the difference, as the data allow it (the original's uses pooled df).
  ci <- tryCatch(t.test(ratio ~ condition, data = s)$conf.int, error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(ci)) out else mutate(out, ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2])
}

# Side-by-side figure: mean fixation ratio by fixation source with 95% CIs, for any number of
# studies (each a group_summary()-shaped tibble), in the order given.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(half = qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * sd / sqrt(n),
           low = pmax(0, mean - half), high = pmin(1, mean + half),
           Condition = factor(condition_labels[condition], levels = condition_labels),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Condition, y = mean, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Fixation source", y = "Concepts rated similar to the initial concept", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
have_scores <- have_data && !is.null(phase1$scores)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r, missing = "not yet collected") {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Self-generated M (SD)` = missing, `Provided M (SD)` = "",
                  `Difference` = "", `95% CI` = "", F = "", p = "", d = "", `Partial η²` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Self-generated M (SD)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", r$m_control, r$sd_control),
         `Provided M (SD)`       = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", r$m_example, r$sd_example),
         `Difference` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", as.integer(r$df_error), r$F),
         p = r$p_text,
         d = sprintf("%.2f", r$d),
         `Partial η²` = sprintf("%.3f", r$partial_eta2))
}
phase_row <- function(study, have, d) {
  if (!have) return(fmt_row(study, NULL))
  fmt_row(study, key_stats(d), missing = if (is.null(d$scores)) "awaiting coding" else "too few analysed")
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", key_original()),
  phase_row("Phase 1: replication", have_data, phase1),
  phase_row("Phase 2: extension", have_phase2, phase2)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrlllrr",
               caption = "Key comparison: main effect of fixation source on the fixation ratio (share of brainstormed concepts rated similar to the initial concept), from the 2 × 2 problem × fixation source ANOVA. Difference = self-generated minus provided example; positive is the original's direction. The original's CI and d assume equal group sizes, which the paper does not report.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

My research is surrounding the design process (often specific to visual design) and design methodology for technology. Therefore, I thought of this paper, which explores the effects of using initial examples on design fixation. I recreated the experiment testing the authors’ first hypothesis: “Providing Examples Leads to More Fixation.” The stimuli in this experiment was to provide participants with an initial design. The control group must come up with their own initial design. Participants are given one of two design problems: either to design a no-spill cup, or a bike rack. My experimental design is a shortened form of the original design in order to preserve resources. Afterwards, each participant’s concept sets were scored by an independent coder (blind to the study hypothesis) on “overall similarity to the initial concept in the set.” I preregistered a 2x2 ANOVA to compare fixation scores across both design problems. I expect properly transforming this workshop-style experiment into a web application to be a bit challenging. I’m thinking an interesting possible extension would be to expand the population of this study to expert designers to see if that changes the results.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# Power to detect the original main effect of fixation source, approximated as a two-group
# comparison (self-generated vs provided) with the original's Cohen's d.
orig_key <- key_original()
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = orig_key$d, sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 2 * ceiling(n))
})

original_effect <- orig_key$estimate
# 2.5 times the original sample, per fixation-source group (Simonsohn, 2015).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$groups$n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per fixation-source group", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect of fixation source (fixation ratio %.2f self-generated vs %.2f provided, d = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original$groups$mean[1], original$groups$mean[2], orig_key$d))
```

Because of resource constraints, I did not follow a power analysis and instead recruited **36 participants** for this study.

### Planned sample

I recruited 36 participants who are preselected on Prolific to be students studying engineering. My stopping rule is to collect until 36 participants pass the exclusion
criteria below:

- Participant has at least one non-empty concept sheet.
- Participant has at least one non-"illegible or uninterpretable" concept sheet (needs to be maunally checked by me).
- Participant has a non-empty inital concept sheet (if they are in the control group).

### Materials

#### 2. Design problems

Design problems were intially presented to the participants in text form. The texts used for these problems were quoted verbatim from the original experiment.

- **No-spill cup:** "Design a disposable, spill-proof coffee cup. The design should be operable with one hand, durable and should not include a mouthpiece or straw."
- **Bike rack:** "Design a car-mounted bicycle rack that addresses the following needs: (1) Easy mounting of the bicycle, (2) Easy mounting of the rack, (3) Cannot harm bike or car, and (4) Must be versatile for all bikes and cars."

#### 3. Example designs with flaw descriptions
Sketches of the inital designs for the no-spill cup and bike rack were presented to the participants along with the above design descriptions in the experimental conditions. These images were copied directly from the paper and presented to the participants are screenshots. Because they are reproductions from the paper, they may be lowere quality than the originals.

Similarly, the flaw descriptions that go along with these images were quoted from the paper as well:

- **No-spill cup:** "Below is an example of a spill proof coffee cup. Please note, the straw will leak when the cup is rotated 90 deg from the angle shown. The cup will leak if squeezed and the hot liquid emerging from the straw will burn one's mouth."

- **Bike rack:** "Below is an example of a present day bike rack. The bicycle is set in the rails and the vinyl coated hook is attached to the seat tube of the bike, and then the hook is tightened down by hand with a wing nut. One should note the difficulty of mounting the middle bikes on the rack."

#### 4. Concept sheets

Concept sheets were provided to the participants during brainstorming. In the original experiment, these sheets had an area for the participant to sketch their idea, then an area to describe their design with the prompt "Describe the concept in detail. How does it work? What are the unique features, mechanisms, and details?" I had adapted this sheet to an online format, where the participant has a drawing box with a pen and undo button, along with a text box for them to describe their design with the same prompt. 

#### 5. Instructional content

Several phases of this study required teaching best practices to the pariticipants. The requried materials for these sections are described below.

- **Introduction to idea generation:** The paper does not give an exact description of how introduces idea generation, so I have summarized based on the paper's description of the content covered.
- **Introduction to individual brainstorming:** This section is provided verbatim in the paper, so I have quoted it exactly in the replication:

> "Brainstorming is a method for generating ideas. When brainstorming on your own:
> 
> 1. Postpone and withhold your judgment of ideas.
> 2. Encourage wild and exaggerated ideas.
> 3. Quantity counts at this stage, not quality.
> 4. Build consecutively on your ideas.
> 5. Every idea has equal worth."

- **Practice brainstorming:** The practice problem provided to participants in this section is included in the paper, so I have copied it verbatim as well: "design a seating device."

#### 6. Coding materials

After the experiemnt, the participants design ideas were coded on their level of fixation by independent coders. According to the paper, coders were blind to condition ans asked to consider "overall similarity to the initial concept in the set" as similar or not similar. We use to exact save wording.

Note I do not know exactly how I will perform coding at this point. Either I will do it myself or perhaps recruit collegues to help out. 

### Procedure

The total time for this study is approximately **40 minutes**.

#### 1. Consent

**Time:** 30 seconds

The course-provided consent message is presented to the participant. They had the option to consent or not consent. If they chose not to consent, they did not have the option to continue with the study.

#### 2. Welcome

**Time:** 30 seconds

Participants were presented with a welcome message and short description of the study. This was not part of the original study design, but was added in order to provide participants with context.

#### 3. Design problem and initial example

**Time:** 3 minutes

From the original paper:

> "students were introduced to the presented problem. Then, students saw either a provided example concept or they generated their own initial concept on a colored concept sheet for the same time period (6 min)."

I followed this exact description, except using a written format rather than verbal instruction. I also shortened the amount of time allotted to this task in order to preserve resources. 

#### 4. Introduction to idea generation

**Time:** 2 minutes

From the original paper:

> "a short (3 min) introduction to idea generation, including a definition of divergent thinking and the goal of creating multiple, diverse concepts…"; "The instructors did not mention fixation"

I follow this exact description, except the exact introduction is not included, so I create one based on the provided description. I again shortened the amount of time allotted to this task in order to preserve resources. 

#### 5. Introduction to brainstorming

**Time:** 2 minutes

From the original paper:

> "A short (3 min) introduction to brainstorming… modified for an individual designer"

I follow this exact description and used the same wording as in the original experiment. But I again shortened the amount of time for this section.

#### 6. Brainstorming practice

**Time:** 2 minutes

From the original paper:

> "Students practiced this idea generation method on a practice problem ('design a seating device') for 3 min."

Again the time allotted to this section is shortened and converted to an online format, but otherwise they follow the same procedure as in the original experiment.

#### 7. Brainstorming

**Time:** 25 minutes

From the original paper:

> "students were asked to create concepts for their assigned design problem using individual brainstorming for 30 min. Students were free to follow the Individual Brainstorming method presented or to use another method (such as natural ideation)."

Again the time allotted to this section is shortened and converted to an online format, but otherwise they follow the same procedure as in the original experiment.

#### 8. Debrief

**Time:** 30 seconds

Participants were presented with a thank you message. This was not part of the original study design, but was added in order to provide participants with context.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** In order to compare the  control group (self-generated inital example), to the experimental group, I use a 2x2 ANOVA across these two conditions and the two design problems. This is the exact measure taken in the original experiment:

> "a 2 × 2 ANOVA with problem and fixation source as between group variables, and the ratio of similar concepts to total number of concepts per student… as the dependent measure."

**Exclusions.** The original study excluded participants via the following criteria:

> "failed to follow instructions or the completed concepts were illegible or uninterpretable"

I expanded this explustion criteria to exclude:

- Participants who didn't complete the study.
- Pariticpants with no non-empty brainstorming concept sheets.
- Control participants with an empty initial concept sheet (in this case there is nothing to compare to).

**Data cleaning.** Empty concept sheets will be dropped from the analysis. This matches the original experiment, where only filled-out sheets were inspected during analysis.

**Data coding.** This experiment has the added task of coding the results of participants' brainstormed concepts on how similar they were to the intial example. In the original experiment:

> "Two independent coders… rated the overall similarity of each generated concept to that student's initial concept (either provided or self-generated)."

They were given the following instructions:

> "The coders were instructed to provide a holistic rating for every concept in the set based on its 'overall similarity to the initial concept in the set.'"
Ratings were "similar" or "not similar".

These coders were blind to the study hypothesis and concepts were presented in a random order. 

In order to preserve resources, I have coded the concept sheets myself, blind to condition.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 185 incoming engineering students, aged 17–18, not paid; 166 analysed. | Students studying engineering on Prolific. | Possibly. Prolific participants may include fewer design novices (not controlled for age), which could potentially lead to less design fixation |
| Sample size | 166 analysed. | 36 participants. | Yes. This experiemnt is very low-powered and therefore not reliable. |
| Setting | In person at a workshop, within rooms with 2 trained proctors | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer. | Attention and distractions may lead to lower quality results. |
| Medium | Paper sheets with descriptions and sections to fill out. | Typed descriptions, and mouse and trackpad skatches. | Drawing with the mouse may have more friction than drawing on paper. | 
| Instruction delivery | Short lessons given by the two proctors. | Self-paced test screens. | This may effect whether the instructions are fully understood by participants (i.e. there's no way for them to ask questions). |
| Phase timings | Everyone is given 6 / 3 / 3 / 3 / 30 min for each of the original experiment sections. |  / 2 / 2 / 3 / 25 min maximums per original section; participants can move on early if they'd like. | Yes. I have shortened their expose to the inital example and given them less time to digest and understand all tasks. |
| Revisiting sheets | Not stated if the participants can revisit their concept sheets. | Any sheet can be edited at any time. | Maybe a small effect if people can go back an differentiate earlier concepts. |
| Access to the initial concept during brainstorming | Not stated if the users have access to the initial example during brainstorming. | Not visible after it is intially shown to pariticpants. | Yes. If the participant can continuously look at their intial exaample, they may fixate more. |
| Coding | Coding	Two coders (a senior undergraduate and a master's student), third coder for disagreements. | Potentially just me, unless I can get help. | Yes, I may be unreliable because I am not blind to the experiment's hypothesis. |

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_scores
cell_means <- scores |>
  group_by(`Fixation source` = condition_labels[as.character(condition)],
           Problem = if_else(problem == "cup", "No-spill cup", "Bike rack")) |>
  summarise(n = n(), M = mean(ratio), SD = sd(ratio), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(cell_means, digits = 2, caption = "Fixation ratio by cell.")

if (nrow(scores) > 4 && n_distinct(scores$condition) == 2) {
  fixation_anova(scores) |>
    transmute(Effect = effect, F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", as.integer(df_error), F),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001), `Partial η²` = sprintf("%.3f", partial_eta2)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "2 × 2 between-subjects ANOVA on the fixation ratio (Type II sums of squares). Original: fixation source F(1, 165) = 4.4, p < .04; problem F(1, 165) = 5.6, p < .02; interaction F < 1.")
} else {
  message("ANOVA not run: it needs analysed participants in both fixation-source groups; there are ", nrow(scores), ".")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_scores
orig <- key_original()
rep  <- key_stats(phase1)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (self-generated − provided)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              d = sprintf("%.2f", d), p = p_text) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in mean fixation ratio, self-generated minus provided example. The original's CI and d assume equal group sizes.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each fixation-source group.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_scores
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_scores
#| fig-cap: "Mean fixation ratio (share of brainstormed concepts rated similar to the initial concept) by fixation source, original study (Leahy et al., 2020, Hypothesis 1 results) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals; the original's assume equal group sizes."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original$groups, `Phase 1: replication` = group_summary(scores))
```

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per fixation-source group in Phase 2

p1_stats <- if (have_data) key_stats(phase1)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(sd = sqrt((p1_stats$sd_control^2 + p1_stats$sd_example^2) / 2), d = p1_stats$d, source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(sd = sqrt((original$groups$sd[1]^2 + original$groups$sd[2]^2) / 2), d = orig_key$d, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the difference in mean fixation ratio at n per group.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, 2 * n - 2) * basis$sd * sqrt(2 / n)
power_at <- function(n, d) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = d, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f (expected)", half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate (difference in mean fixation ratio), Phase 2 expected values based on the SD in %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: d = %.2f", orig_key$d),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: d = %.2f", p1_stats$d),
                         sprintf("Half the original: d = %.2f", orig_key$d / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_key$d),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, abs(p1_stats$d)),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_key$d / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per fixation-source group, two-sided alpha = .05 (two-group approximation).", phase2_n_per_group))
```
